books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

primary_sources: Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from a Birmingham Jail, April 16, 1963 (paraphrased)
Civil Rights Act of 1964, Public Law 88-352 (paraphrased)
Stokely Carmichael, speech at Greenwood, Mississippi, June 16, 1966 (paraphrased)
U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, Political Participation (1968)

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the table is from the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights; the photograph is public domain

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the civil rights movement changed the lives of Black Americans from 1960 to 1968.

documents.title: Four students sit down
documents.source: Account of the Greensboro sit-ins, February 1, 1960, drawn from the grounding books.
documents.sourcing: The account describes the first sit-in from the students' side, so it shows the tactic as the students themselves understood it.
documents.text: On February 1, 1960, four Black freshmen from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College sat at the whites-only lunch counter of a Woolworth's store in Greensboro, North Carolina, and asked to be served. They were refused and stayed in their seats until the store closed. Within weeks students in other Southern cities held sit-ins of their own.

documents.title: Testing the law on the buses
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Congress of Racial Equality's account of the Freedom Rides, 1961.
documents.sourcing: CORE organized the rides, so its account stresses the purpose of testing the law rather than the violence that followed.
documents.text: In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality sent Black and white riders together on buses through the South to test whether the Supreme Court's ruling against segregated bus terminals was being enforced. Near Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of the buses. The Interstate Commerce Commission then ordered segregation ended in interstate bus terminals, effective November 1, 1961.

documents.title: Why we cannot wait
documents.source: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from a Birmingham Jail, written April 16, 1963.
documents.sourcing: King writes from a jail cell to white clergymen who urged him to wait, so he defends direct action to an audience that favors patience.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from a Birmingham Jail, April 16, 1963. King answered white clergymen who had urged him to let the local political system address racial injustice. He wrote that "'Wait' has almost always meant 'Never'," and that the Black community had waited long enough for change.

documents.title: Marching for jobs and freedom
documents.source: Photograph: March on Washington, August 28, 1963, public domain (U.S. federal government photograph, National Archives).
documents.sourcing: The photograph shows the march as the marchers presented it, with their own signs stating their demands.

documents.title: The law changes
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Public Law 88-352, signed July 2, 1964.
documents.sourcing: The act is a law, so its words show what Congress required, not only what the movement hoped for.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, signed July 2, 1964. The act banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. Title II barred segregation in public accommodations such as hotels, restaurants, and theaters. Title VII barred discrimination in employment and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

documents.title: Registration rises
documents.source: Table: African American voter registration, percent of voting-age population, U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, Political Participation (1968).
documents.sourcing: The table comes from a federal commission report, so it measures the Voting Rights Act's results rather than arguing for the act.
documents.text: African American voter registration, percent of voting-age population. Mississippi: 6.7% in 1964, 59.8% in 1967. Alabama: 23.0% in 1964, 51.6% in 1967. Georgia: 27.4% in 1964, 52.6% in 1967. Louisiana: 31.6% in 1964, 58.9% in 1967. South Carolina: 37.3% in 1964, 51.2% in 1967. Virginia: 38.3% in 1964, 55.6% in 1967.

documents.title: A new slogan
documents.source: Paraphrase of Stokely Carmichael, speech at Greenwood, Mississippi, June 16, 1966.
documents.sourcing: Carmichael speaks to a rally of marchers on the Meredith March, so he states the new slogan in its most forceful form to rally a crowd.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Stokely Carmichael, Greenwood, Mississippi, June 16, 1966. Carmichael told the crowd, "We been saying freedom for six years and we ain't got nothin'. What we got to start saying now is Black Power!" He later explained that Black Power meant Black people uniting, recognizing their heritage, building community, and defining their own goals.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent of the change or of federal advance, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Jim Crow South, the Cold War pressure on American democracy, or the postwar growth of federal power.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (first point): earns the point for describing specific examples from at least three documents that support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (outside evidence): earns the point for describing at least one specific piece of evidence beyond the documents that supports the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating a document's content as outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience of at least one document shapes what it says.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how that shapes the document does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing a complex understanding, such as explaining both change and continuity, or qualifying the argument with evidence that cuts the other way.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument with no qualification or counter-evidence does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The movement changed Black lives greatly in law and voting by 1968, but much less in daily economic life, so the change was real and unfinished.
Grouping: Documents 1-4 show grassroots pressure (sit-ins, Freedom Rides, Letter, March); Documents 5-6 show legal and voting gains (Civil Rights Act, registration table); Document 7 shows the turn to Black Power.
Outside evidence: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register voters; the Kerner Commission in 1968 blamed poverty and segregation for the urban riots.
Complexity: The same movement that won the 1964 and 1965 laws produced Black Power, because legal victories did not end poverty or everyday segregation, so the argument qualifies the change it claims.
